claims.claim: A hypothetical counterexample may be assumed to contain the empty set and to have ground set equal to the union of its members.
claims.evidence: The finite union U of all members belongs to F by repeated union closure, and deleting points outside U changes no member or active frequency. If ∅ is absent, adjoining it preserves union closure and all frequencies; a strict inequality d_x<|F|/2 remains strict after the family size increases by one.

claims.claim: Equivalent active elements can be identified without changing the number of members or any relevant frequency.
claims.evidence: Every member is a union of incidence-equivalence classes. Projecting to one representative per active class commutes with union and preserves class frequencies. It is injective because two distinct members differ on a whole equivalence class, so the number of members is unchanged.

claims.claim: If any counterexample exists, then a counterexample containing ∅ and having odd cardinality exists.
claims.evidence: First adjoin ∅ if necessary. If the resulting counterexample has even size 2k, remove a minimum-cardinality nonempty member S. No two remaining members can have union S, since every nonempty subset of S belonging to the family has size at least |S| and hence equals S. Frequencies remain at most k−1, which is below (2k−1)/2. The only case in which no nonempty member would remain is {∅,S}, which is not a counterexample.

claims.claim: A union-closed family containing a singleton satisfies Frankl’s bound.
claims.evidence: For {x}∈F, the map A↦A∪{x} injects members avoiding x into members containing x. Its image lies in F by union closure, so at least half the family contains x.

claims.claim: A union-closed family containing a two-element member satisfies Frankl’s bound.
claims.evidence: For {x,y}∈F, union with {x,y} injects the cell containing neither element into the cell containing both. Consequently d_x+d_y≥|F|, so one of x,y has frequency at least |F|/2.

claims.claim: Every separating union-closed family on n active elements has an element of frequency at least n; hence it satisfies Frankl’s bound whenever |F|≤2n.
claims.evidence: Order frequencies d_1≤⋯≤d_n. For i<j, separation and the frequency order ensure a member contains x_j but not x_i. Thus M_i, the union of all members avoiding x_i, exists, excludes x_i, and contains x_{i+1},…,x_n. The distinct members M_1,…,M_{n−1},X all contain x_n, proving d_n≥n. If |F|≤2n, this is at least |F|/2.

claims.claim: For a separating family containing ∅, an exact incidence lower bound is available.
claims.evidence: With m=|F|, minimum positive size r, and T=Σ_A|A|, the canonical members X,M_1,…,M_{n−1} have total size at least n+Σ_{k=1}^{n−1}max(r,k). Every other member except ∅ has size at least r. Hence T≥n(n+1)/2+r(r−1)/2+r(m−n−1). The n=1 edge case gives F={∅,{x}} and satisfies the same formula with equality.

claims.claim: Frankl’s conjecture holds whenever the smallest positive member of the reduced family has size r≥n/2. In particular, it holds for every family with at most six inequivalent active elements.
claims.evidence: For the lower bound L in claim 6, 2L−nm=(2r−n)(m−n−1)+r(r−1)≥0 when r≥n/2, so average frequency is at least m/2. Conversely, a reduced counterexample would have r≥3 by the singleton and two-set results but r<n/2 by this inequality. Those conditions require n≥7, excluding every family with at most six inequivalent active elements.

claims.claim: A normalized separating counterexample with parameters n,m,r must have odd m and satisfy an explicit quantitative lower bound.
claims.evidence: Oddness follows from claim 2 before quotienting. In an odd counterexample, every frequency is at most (m−1)/2, so T≤n(m−1)/2. Combining this with claim 6 gives (n−2r)m≥n(n+2−2r)+r²−3r. Since claim 7 gives n−2r>0, division is valid. Claim 5 independently gives m≥2n+1, yielding exactly the stated maximum of the two lower bounds.

claims.claim: Any normalized separating counterexample on seven elements must have at least 25 members.
claims.evidence: For n=7, the preceding results force r=3 and odd m≥21. At m=21, equality in both incidence bounds makes all frequencies 10 and forces M_2={x_3,…,x_7}; closure then gives F_{x_1}⊆F_{x_2}, and equal frequencies contradict separation. At m=23, if M_2 has size five, separation and the frequency cap force the sole vector (10,11,11,11,11,11,11), while at most six members can contain x_1. If M_2=X\{x_2}, equality forces the stated M_5 and M_6, and only 10 further triples are compatible with union by M_3 although 15 are required. The checker exhaustively confirmed all integer and finite configuration counts.
claims.search_method: Exact enumeration of admissible r,m values, ordered frequency vectors, canonical M_5/M_6 choices, and compatible triples in the m=21 and m=23 equality cases.

claims.claim: Frankl’s bound holds if the family is closed under both unions and intersections.
claims.evidence: After adjoining ∅ if necessary, choose an inclusion-minimal nonempty A and x∈A. If U avoids x, intersection closure makes U∩A a proper member below A, so U∩A=∅. The map U↦U∪A then injects members avoiding x into members containing x. Removing the adjoined ∅, if any, only lowers the required threshold.

claims.claim: Exact enumeration verifies Frankl’s conjecture for every labelled ground set of size at most five and verifies the tight-clean power-set conclusion there.
claims.evidence: The exact bitmask enumerator found respectively 4, 14, 122, 4,960, and 2,771,104 union-closed families for n=1,…,5, with zero Frankl violations. For every n it found exactly one tight clean family containing ∅, namely the full power set, and no tight clean non-power-set. Direct enumeration of all 2^(2^n) assignments independently reproduced the counts through n=4. The descending-size branching is exhaustive because every union required when a set is included has already been decided; any forbidden union of two later sets is detected when the second is included.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive exact integer-bitmask enumeration for n≤5, with independent direct-assignment cross-checking for n≤4.

claims.claim: The natural strengthening “every smallest nonempty member contains a Frankl element” is false.
claims.evidence: The checker verified 19 distinct members, all 361 ordered-pair unions, minimum positive size three, and frequencies (9,9,9,14,14,14,17). Thus the minimum member {1,2,3} contains no element occurring in at least half of the 19 members, while the family itself remains union-closed.
claims.search_method: Exact seven-bit encoding; exhaustive ordered-pair union testing and integer frequency counting.

target_evidence: The exact target asks for either a proof of Frankl’s conjecture for every finite union-closed family or an explicit counterexample. The draft expressly states that it obtains neither, and none of its claims closes the unrestricted case. All listed claims nevertheless survive independent audit and give material partial progress: reductions on possible counterexamples, proofs for several substantial subclasses, quantitative restrictions through seven reduced elements, exhaustive verification through five labelled elements, and a verified obstruction to a natural strengthening. Therefore the target coverage is VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS, the declared resolution PARTIAL is ACCURATE, and the final writeup does not overclaim full resolution.
